units.function: Cryptographic unit tests for locally minted Agent run JWTs, including run/responsible-user/scope claims, expiry, issuer/audience validation, Company- and instance-derived keys and optional legacy master-secret verification.
units.dependencyDirection: The local runtime token helper reads process-level signing configuration, derives an HMAC key from control-plane instance and Company identifiers, signs Agent/run claims and verifies them before middleware constructs a request actor.
units.keyDataModels: Agent subject, Company, Adapter type, run id, responsible user, skill-test scope, instance id, issuer/audience, issued/expiry times and legacy-fallback policy.
units.lifecycle: Minted tokens default to a one-hour lifetime and are bound by claims and signature to one Company and control-plane instance. Missing signing configuration disables mint/verify. Issuer, audience, expiration, claim tampering and cross-instance use are rejected. A configurable compatibility path accepts tokens signed directly with the shared master secret; it can be disabled while derived-key tokens continue to work.
units.testAssessment: Sixteen focused cryptographic cases cover normal and scoped tokens, missing/fallback secrets, expiry, issuer/audience, Company and instance isolation, tampering, TTL and legacy-floor behavior. Missing are key identifiers/rotation overlap, asymmetric signing or KMS, jti/revocation, not-before/clock skew, algorithm-confusion/invalid JSON/oversize cases, claim schema validation, Agent/run lifecycle revocation, responsible-human status changes and proof that a token cannot cross deployment profile or Connector instance.
units.designRationale: Give local Agent processes short-lived delegated access without database lookup for every signature check, while limiting a shared secret's direct tenant/instance reach and preserving an upgrade path for already issued tokens.
units.companyOsProblem: Company OS needs short-lived, audience-specific runtime attestations that let any Connector act only for an exact Work execution, tenant and approved responsibility/data contract across managed-cloud and local enterprise nodes.
units.companyOsFit: ADAPT the tenant/instance key separation, narrow run scope and strict issuer/audience/expiry checks. Use a versioned RuntimeAttestation with key id, Connector instance, WorkExecution, ResponsibilityContract version, authorization/data-policy digest, jti and short expiry; support rotation and revocation through IdentityPort/KMS. Do not fall back to a human-login secret or tenant-agnostic master signature in production.
units.responsibilityConflict: responsible_user_id is a signed string captured at mint time, not evidence that the human accepted responsibility or remained authorized. The token omits approval, permission, data contract and evidence-policy versions. Legacy master-secret acceptance weakens both Company and instance isolation and can outlive organizational changes until expiry.

units.function: HTTP middleware tests for converting signed Agent JWTs and hashed Agent API keys into request actors, preserving scoped delegation, rejecting run spoofing/cross-instance tokens and enforcing a responsible-user binding.
units.dependencyDirection: ActorMiddleware verifies bearer credentials, reads Agent/API-key/heartbeat-run rows for compatibility and status context, writes authentication-denial ActivityLog rows, then downstream route authorization consumes the normalized Agent actor and Company scope.
units.keyDataModels: Agent actor/source, signed run/responsible-user/skill-test claims, optional run header, Agent API key hash/revocation/scope/responsible user, heartbeat run attribution and authentication-denial activity.
units.lifecycle: A valid run JWT produces an Agent actor whose signed run id and responsible user are authoritative; skill-test scope survives. A mismatched run header is rejected with a structured code and audited. Legacy claim-less tokens use the run row's responsible user. Cross-instance tokens fail before protected reads/writes. Agent keys inherit their stored responsible-user binding, while keys without one are denied and audited.
units.testAssessment: Seven route-level cases cover signed-claim precedence, scoped delegation, spoof detection/audit, legacy attribution, instance isolation, API-key attribution and fail-closed missing responsibility. Missing are revoked/expired keys, inactive/deleted Agent or human, key scope enforcement, Company/run/Agent row mismatch, changed responsibility after mint, concurrent revocation, board/session ambiguity, token replay, audit-write failure, timing leakage and end-to-end permission/data-policy checks.
units.designRationale: Normalize multiple non-human credential forms into one downstream authorization actor while ensuring caller-supplied headers cannot replace signed run identity and every durable Agent key has a human attribution anchor.
units.companyOsProblem: Company OS must authenticate technical Agents and then separately prove their current delegated authority, exact Work binding and accountable human before any data read or effectful action.
units.companyOsFit: ADAPT the signed-claim authority, header mismatch denial/audit, scoped actor projection and fail-closed missing human binding. Add a current authorization check against immutable ResponsibilityContract and WorkExecution versions, active human/Agent/Connector status, permission and data-policy digests, token jti revocation and action-specific scope. Authentication denial audit must use a resilient append-only security sink.
units.responsibilityConflict: The middleware equates a token/API-key responsible-user value with current accountability and does not show acceptance, employment status or contract version checks. A legacy database fallback derives responsibility after the fact, while a still-valid token may continue to name an offboarded or superseded human. Technical authentication alone cannot authorize enterprise data use or high-risk effects.
